journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: How South African undergraduate first-generation university students choose an elective academic literacy module in the absence of comparative information: A case study of one comprehensive university in Johannesburg
abstract: Entering university entails programme and module choices that can foster or hinder a student’s academic success and future career. This paper argues that, in the absence of adequate information, South African undergraduate first-generation university students’ (FGSs) choice of an elective academic literacy (AL) module is strongly influenced by its perceived relevance to their field of study. This article was theoretically grounded in the disciplinary literacy perspectives of Moje (2008) and Shanahan and Shanahan (2008). The research assumed a qualitative perspective. The study entailed a single case study design because the aim was to gain insights into FGSs’ AL module selection strategies at the selected university. The methodology used pre-module semi-structured individual interviews as a data collection technique. The thematic analysis of interview transcripts and the document analysis of the case-study module, English for Law (EFL), constituted the data scrutiny procedures. The research generated significant findings. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Confronting early bullying: The transformative role of foundation phase teachers in fostering inclusive and conducive classrooms
abstract: Bullying behaviours often emerge during early childhood yet are frequently minimised or normalised in Foundation Phase classrooms, limiting opportunities for early intervention. Foundation Phase teachers are therefore strategically positioned to identify, address, and prevent bullying during its formative stages. This qualitative study explores the preparedness of Foundation Phase pre-service teachers to respond to bullying during school-based learning in South African primary schools. Guided by a humanising theoretical framework, the study involved 60 third-year pre-service teachers enrolled in a Bachelor of Education programme at a South African university. Data were generated through reflective narrative essays and analysed using critical thematic analysis. The findings indicate that bullying manifests in verbal, physical, and relational forms and is shaped by broader socio-economic inequalities, overcrowding, and limited institutional support. The findings inform practical recommendations for classroom practice, teacher education and policy aimed at fostering inclusive and emotionally safe learning environments.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Desired attributes of undergraduate tourism students: An international Delphi academic perspective
abstract: Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) play a critical role in preparing students for the complexities of the modern workforce. While existing research has explored graduate attributes from industry and policy perspectives, limited attention has been given to the views of lecturers, who are central to curriculum design and implementation. This study addresses this gap by employing a qualitative Delphi approach to identify the attributes considered essential for undergraduate tourism students, drawing on insights from an international panel of academic experts. Seven core attributes emerged as fundamental for equipping graduates with the competencies required for professional practice, further study, continuous development and lifelong learning. These findings not only reinforce existing theoretical frameworks but also provide empirical input for curriculum development and transformation. Moreover, they offer a foundation for future research and practice-based inquiry aimed at enhancing the alignment between tourism education and the evolving demands of the global industry.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Scaffolding STEM education through translanguaging
abstract: Incorporating Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education in various African countries is increasingly viewed as a response to the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR). Most students engaging with STEM disciplines in Africa are English as a second language (ESL) speakers, while the medium of instruction remains English. This paper critically examines translanguaging as a potential pedagogical strategy for the effective teaching and learning of STEM subjects within ESL contexts in Zimbabwean secondary schools. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews with 16 science and mathematics teachers who were equitably drawn through purposeful sampling from two rural and two urban secondary schools in Zimbabwe. Two non-participant lesson observations were also conducted at each of the four selected schools. The findings reveal that the incorporation of learners’ first language (L1) in STEM instruction correlates with improved outcomes. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Beyond structure: Cultivating a culture-driven doctoral programme
abstract: For decades, concerns have been raised about the dominance of one-on-one or co-supervision models of postgraduate education in the Humanities and Social Sciences in South Africa. These concerns highlight poor throughput and retention, financial constraints, supervisor capacity challenges, and the isolation experienced by both candidates and supervisors. Using an Appreciative Inquiry lens, this article examines the design of a programme in which 10 university staff members undertook PhD studies focused on social justice and quality in higher education. The programme incorporated coursework, supervision panels, ‘Doc Weeks’, online communities, and regular progress presentations and reporting. The article argues that while such curriculum structures are important, they are insufficient on their own to address challenges in postgraduate education. Instead, the cultural norms and values embedded in the programme, and the ways in which these were made explicit, were central to its success. The findings offer practical insights into structuring a PhD programme and, more importantly, demonstrate the need for these structures to be underpinned by a shared culture. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Editorial
abstract: This editorial introduces the 21st edition of The International Journal of Teaching and Learning (IJTL) with a focus on language as a structural barrier to equitable education. Drawing on international assessment data (PIRLS, TIMSS, PISA) and UNESCO reporting, the editorial argues that teaching learners in a language they do not fully understand significantly undermines academic achievement and perpetuates societal inequality, a challenge particularly acute in multilingual contexts such as South Africa. It further highlights how this barrier intersects with the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, compounding disadvantage for already marginalised learners. Translanguaging is proposed as a promising pedagogical response, enabling multilingual learners to draw on their full linguistic repertoire to support meaning-making and conceptual understanding. The editorial concludes with an overview of the issue's contributions, which span translanguaging in primary and STEM education, first-year higher education experiences, digital and pedagogical innovations, and inclusive learning environments.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Social media applications as pedagogical tools for teaching
abstract: Social media applications are increasingly prevalent, yet their educational potential remains underexplored. While these platforms can enhance communication and collaboration in formal and informal learning environments, their effective integration into education requires further investigation. Guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, this study examines how seven Grade 6 and 7 teachers at a public primary school in Cape Town, South Africa, integrated social media platforms like WhatsApp, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram into their lessons. Although literature highlights the benefits of social media in boosting student motivation and confidence, its role in primary education remains limited. This qualitative case study explored teachers' integration of social media tools and their impact on learning outcomes. Purposive and convenience sampling were used to select participants in a socioeconomically diverse school. Data were gathered through questionnaires, lesson plan analysis, and semi-structured interviews, offering a detailed understanding of teachers' experiences. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Information seeking behaviour among private higher education undergraduate students in a fourth industrial revolution era
abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) era is continuously transforming the higher education landscape. This transformation includes how students access, evaluate, and use information in their academic activities. Despite this, little is known about undergraduate students' information-seeking behaviour, particularly their competence, confidence, and emotional well-being. This descriptive survey investigates this phenomenon at a selected private higher learning institution in South Africa. Data were collected from 145 undergraduate students using a structured questionnaire administered on Google Forms. The findings revealed that 62% of undergraduate students experience uncertainty and anxiety at the beginning of their information-seeking behaviour and that 96% rely on popular search engines like Google rather than scholarly databases. The reason for this is the limited digital literacy skills, such as advanced domain-specific search techniques and unfamiliarity with Boolean logic operators. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Exploring lecturer perceptions of digital curriculum mapping in South African higher education institutions
abstract: Digital curriculum mapping (DCM) serves as an essential technology-enhanced tool and process for curriculum development, facilitating lecturer-student engagement in online learning. DCM can simplify curriculum alignment and enhance lecturers’ pedagogical skills and technological proficiency by addressing longstanding training and cognitive gaps, as well as the need for dynamic implementation practices. However, little research is available on the current state of digital curriculum mapping at South African higher education institutions (SAHEIs), including both public and private institutions, indicating a significant gap in research. The problem was exacerbated during academic forums on curriculum development when it became evident that some institutions lacked sufficient knowledge and experience in digital curriculum mapping, thereby hindering collective digital sharing efforts. The research aim was to explore how lecturers across diverse educational institutions in South Africa perceive and apply curriculum alignment and digital mapping. A qualitative methodological approach was adopted using in-depth interviews with 13 purposefully selected lecturers from four institutions. Them

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Implementing translanguaging pedagogies in a cross-age reading programme with primary school learners in South Africa
abstract: Many South African primary school classrooms remain dominated by monoglossic ideologies, limiting learners’ participation and access to quality education. Research shows that 81% of Grade 4 learners cannot read for meaning across the country’s 11 official languages, highlighting the urgent need to recognise and leverage the language(s) learners bring to the classroom. This study employed a qualitative approach to implement a cross-age reading programme informed by translanguaging pedagogy in a context where English and isiXhosa are traditionally taught separately. Participants included 10 Grade 7 tutors and 10 Grade 3 tutees from a primary school in the Eastern Cape. Data comprised audio-recorded reading sessions, learner-written artefacts, and observation notes. Findings indicate that translanguaging activities enhanced learner engagement, scaffolded comprehension, and supported the development of reading, writing, speaking, and digital literacy skills. By allowing learners to draw on their full linguistic repertoires, the intervention provided meaningful scaffolding and fostered emergent biliteracy. The study recommends the flexible and dynamic use of multiple languages in primar

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Sharing the load: Exploring education postgraduate students’ perceptions and experiences of working collaboratively for assessments in an online distance learning environment
abstract: In Higher Education online and distance Postgraduate (PG) education programmes, working collaboratively is often used as a strategy to promote deeper learning, peer interaction, and critical thinking. However, students’ perceptions and experiences of such collaboration, particularly within the context of formative assessment, remain relatively under-researched. This study explores how PG students in a Faculty of Education experience and perceive working collaboratively to complete and submit formative assessment tasks. The research is grounded in connectivism (Siemens, 2005), which emphasises learning as a networked process occurring through interaction between people and digital tools. Using a qualitative case study approach, data were collected through open-ended questionnaires distributed amongst two cohorts of distance PG students. Thematic analysis was used to interpret the data and reveal key themes related to group dynamics. The findings offer practical insights for lecturers and programme designers seeking to structure more effective and equitable collaborative assessments in online distance PG education.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Seamless learning as an alternative learning and teaching strategy: A case study of a social entrepreneurship module
abstract: Students seem no longer to be satisfied with the traditional ways of teaching and learning. Seamless learning may be a solution to the problem. The research project’s objectives were: first, to propose seamless learning as an alternative teaching and learning tool by providing students with the freedom to learn whenever and wherever they choose through the use of handheld devices; secondly, to measure the success of implementing this strategy through a single case study. The target group was 39 Community Development students. We implemented a qualitative method using biographic questionnaires and interviews comprising open-ended, non-leading questions. Ten students were selected through a random, purposive sampling method. Students experienced the seamless learning approach as positive, forward-thinking and empowering. This research offers an alternative way of presenting knowledge and designing assessments. The study shows that adapting content may lead to more accessible and engaging experiences for students.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Teaching of Mitosis in South African classrooms: Instructional strategies and challenges
abstract: Mitosis is a fundamental biological process that underpins various concepts in Life Sciences (Biology). Consequently, fostering a strong scientific foundation is widely recognised as essential for learners to develop logical reasoning skills. The current study examines the instructional strategies used and challenges faced by teachers in teaching mitosis topics in the FET (Further Education and Training) phase in South African Grade 10 Life Sciences (Biology) classrooms. Eight teachers in one of the circuits of the Gert Sibande District, Mpumalanga Province, participated. An interpretive approach was adopted, with the conceptual framework of pedagogical content knowledge guiding the research. Interview data underwent content analysis, while thematic analysis was used for the lesson observation data. The study identified a deficiency in creative, topic-specific instructional strategies, particularly those incorporating technology. Additionally, the study revealed that teachers struggled with mitosis-related content and terminology, demonstrating limited pedagogical content knowledge. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Restoring student agency in post-digital visualisation: An action research project, 2020-2024.
abstract: Digitising interior design visuals often produces hyper-realistic renders generated through highly specialised programs to simulate utopian design solutions. These digital representations are lauded by their creators but criticised for their homogeneity, lack of context, and lack of visual narrative. This lack of distinctive visual identity is attributed to the prevalence of technological determinism, which views technological mastery as innately superior. Nonetheless, students can be exposed to alternative visualisation models through the post-digital paradigm to counter this determinist mindset. The post-digital approach provides a critical lens on technology's role in visualisation and reintroduces affective digital-making practices. It shifts the focus away from technological advancements and challenges technological deterministic optimism. Post-digital thinking enhances student agency, helping to foreground 'designerly' and individual identity and decentralising digital acumen. To explore this, we initiated an action research project investigating the benefits of the post-digital paradigm in the interior design studio. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Utilising ICT for classroom teaching and learning: Practices among South African teachers.
abstract: This research considered South African primary school teachers’ use of Information Communication and Technology (ICTs) in the domains of English First Additional Language, mathematics, and natural sciences. Utilising the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study explored what ICTs are being used for assessment purposes and how ICTs are being used. Employing a mixed-method approach within a pragmatist paradigm, a survey designed by the researchers was administered to teachers with a minimum of five years of experience. Quantitative analysis of closed-ended questions revealed that commonly used ICT tools included personal computers, the internet, intranet, and mobile devices, whereas outdated technologies like CDs and DVDs were seldom utilised. Surprisingly, newer ICTs, such as WhatsApp, were not as frequently employed as anticipated. Qualitative insights demonstrated that teachers harnessed ICTs for various functions, including formative and summative assessments, multimedia learning, personalised learning, resource discovery, engagement with educational platforms, and document handling. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: South African Business Studies teachers’ implementation of case-based teaching method in technology-enhanced classrooms to promote learner participation
abstract: Learner participation in their learning is important to foster meaningful learning. Thus, teachers adopt different teaching methods including case-based teaching method to propel learners’ participation in learning. This qualitative study explored business studies teachers’ implementation of case-based teaching in technology-enhanced classrooms. The study is located within the interpretivists’ paradigm and utilises Experiential Learning Theory as a lens to interpret and thematically analyse interviews collected from six business studies teachers, from six secondary schools in KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa that were selected purposefully. The study found that a case-based teaching method is compatible with technology integration and helps teachers to expose learners to real business situations. Consequently, integrating technology while implementing case-based teaching transforms the learning context. It is recommended that business studies teachers intensify the implementation of case-based teaching in their technology-enhanced classrooms to facilitate learners’ understanding as they participate in learning.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Editorial
abstract: Vast leaps in technological advancements have placed us firmly in the middle of the 4th Industrial Revolution (4IR) with elements of the 5th (5IR) already in play. The 4IR may be characterised by the integration of digital technologies with physical systems, creating cyber-physical systems, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), big data and analytics, Artificial Intelligence (AI) with automation in manufacturing processes and chatbots in call centres. The 5IR builds on the 4IR through inter alia collaboration between humans and machines (cobots), agentic AIs, creation of personalised products and services and the integration of technologies in areas such as human health. These have far implications for persons as they strive for personal growth and fulfilment. Education plays a particularly important role in achieving these, making the need for inclusive and innovative quality education provision more urgent than ever. The impact of technological advancements is already being felt in the labour market. For some, AI carries out dreary tasks, allowing space for creativity. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: The influence of hybrid problem-based learning on Senior Phase preservice Technology teachers’ self-directed learning abilities
abstract: Hybrid problem-based learning (hPBL) may promote the ability of students to learn independently. This paper explores the impact of hPBL on preservice Technology teachers’ self-directed learning (SDL) abilities. In this case study, a mixed-methods research design was used. The self-directed learning instrument (SDLI) developed by Cheng and colleagues was used to collect quantitative data. For the qualitative data observations, semi-structured individual interviews and self-reflective journals of preservice Technology teachers were used to give more meaning to the quantitative results. In this study, hPBL had positive influences on preservice Technology teachers’ SDL abilities. Employing hPBL had a slightly positive impact on ‘planning and implementation’ as an SDL sub-domain. The preservice teachers’ self-monitoring abilities increased statistically significantly. In addition, the hPBL intervention contributed to a slight improvement in the interpersonal communication abilities of these preservice Technology teachers. It is recommended that hPBL be implemented in larger classes in Technology Education, as well as in longitudinal studies to determine the long-term impact of hPBL on p

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: The role of emerging Artificial Intelligence in the establishment of inclusive learning environments
abstract: Students with learning difficulties face significant challenges in accessing equitable education. Integrating emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) can address students’ diverse learning needs and promote inclusivity. This quantitative study explored the role of AI-driven technologies in fostering inclusive learning environments for students, including those with difficulties. Using random sampling, 180 South African Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) college respondents completed a five-point Likert scale questionnaire. The findings showed that AI integration holds significant possibilities to enhance inclusivity but is hindered by challenges such as the digital divide, limited digital skills among instructors, and concerns over data privacy and academic integrity. The study recommended targeted investments in ICT infrastructure in underserved areas, professional development to strengthen educators’ digital competencies, active stakeholder involvement in AI development, and the establishment of ethical frameworks to ensure the secure handling of sensitive data in education. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Using digital technology in Design and Technology pedagogy to support the attainment of 21st century skills by senior secondary students in Botswana
abstract: Technology-based learning and the development of 21st century skills have the potential to transform the traditional teacher-centred approach into a more student-centred approach. Digital technology integration can be harnessed to foster effective learning and teaching. This study utilised the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) theoretical framework and explores the utilisation of digital technology in the learning and teaching of Design and Technology (D&T) in Botswana’s senior secondary schools, with the aim of fostering the development of 21st century skills among students. The study adopted a case study that involves the collection of data from school heads, teachers and students through a survey. The findings indicate that 83.3% of school heads were somewhat satisfied with available digital technology resources in schools. The study reveals that 37.5% of the D&T students who perceive their teachers as possessing critical thinking skills are good at using digital technology resources during the lesson. This implies that it is imperative to recognise the importance of leveraging the pedagogical benefits of integrating digital technology toimpart 21st century ski

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Navigating higher education student success: Reflective narrative lessons from a South African university
abstract: Student success is vital to higher education (HE) stakeholders, regardless of how it is measured or defined, highlighting the need for efficient pedagogic practices to successfully achieve intended educational and student outcomes. This research comprises examples of sound pedagogical practices from the success stories of teaching academics in a Humanities Faculty. It explores characteristics of practices that could enhance academic performance and foster student success by analysing eight (n=8) Humanities lecturers' successes in university teaching experiences. The qualitative narrative inquiry used semi-structured interviews, narrative analysis methods, and a reflective narrative analysis lens to unpack some distinctive features of impactful higher education pedagogies from South African higher education settings. Theories of reflection frame the study, permitting reflection, narration, and sharing of instructive approaches based on critical reflection. Findings suggest that the purposeful, selective use of learning tools and integration into apt working student-centred practices positively impact undergraduate learning, academic performance and success.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Self-determination and undergraduate student success: A view from high performing students in a South African university
abstract: Using self-determination as a theoretical perspective, the study sought to understand the motivating factors behind high-performing students’ success. High-performing students who are on track for cum laude and summa cum laude were identified as the cohort for the study. A sample of 10 of these identified students was purposively selected from the School of Education at a South African university. Data were generated using individual and focus group interviews. The findings suggest that these students were motivated by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. The students were intrinsically motivated when their needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness were met. The findings further suggest that three levels of extrinsic motivation (introjected, identified and integrated regulation) influenced students’ success. The study challenges a deficit discourse as it enabled us to understand the factors that enabled high-performing students to thrive despite social and economic hardships. These views from high-performing students’ are useful to inform strategies and interventions for understanding and improving undergraduate student success.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Crossing the border: Gendered experiences of immigrant children in South African schools
abstract: The study examines how the family, peers, and sociocultural environment at school in primary schools in South Africa perpetuated divergent gendered experiences among immigrant learners. A qualitative narrative inquiry was used during the study. Snowball sampling was used to select the participants for the study. The study drew on a narrative account of 27 participants, 18 immigrant children (9 girls and 9 boys) and nine teachers (6 women and 3 men) from three primary schools in the Johannesburg East District. Semi-structured in-depth interviews and observations were used as instruments to collect data from the participants. Collected data from the semi-structured, in-depth interviews and observations was analysed using thematic content analysis and was presented by using illustrative quotes. The study revealed that the school is a highly gendered place and serves to propagate gendered experiences among immigrant children in school between girls and boys. The findings of the study have significant implications for stake holders at all levels in education. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Cultivating socially just responsible citizens in relation to university accounting education in South Africa
abstract: The aim of this study – situated within the particular South African context that has been marred by systemic inequality and social injustice – was to determine whether higher education institutions could cultivate and nurture socially responsible democratic citizens. Secondary research questions focused on the required teaching and learning practices that support democratic citizenship education, and on the identity of the university educator responsible for implementing these teaching and learning practices. In particular, the focus was on the advantages of utilising deliberative encounters as a pedagogical strategy in higher education. In the development of the study, the emphasis particularly shifted to the consideration of whether deliberative encounters could assist in cultivating socially responsible chartered accountants. The research approach used was pragmatism, which was appropriate to focus on the possible responses to existing societal problems. Within this framework, deconstruction was applied as method in order to determine whether any marginalised voices were absent from this particular discourse. Through applying Foucault’s genealogical analysis to the chartered ac

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Student volunteer experiences as a way to advance teaching and learning: a call for community service
abstract: This paper makes a case to advance community service through teaching and learning at higher education institutions in South Africa. In particular, it highlights the benefits of student volunteerism as one pathway to engagement and promotion of social responsibility amongst students. The data are drawn from a qualitative, exploratory study undertaken with a sample of 14 students at Durban University of Technology, who participated in volunteering at different community organisations and schools during their undergraduate studies. The study found that students benefitted from this experience and believed that the university had a salient role to play in community engagement. The article concludes with an argument for academics to reconsider communities as learning spaces and to begin to advance community engagement in other ways through teaching.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: A framework for the development and improvement of computational thinking for high school learners using a programming language and learner management system
abstract: Many educational departments are losing the battle against inefficient mathematics education. The Annual National Assessments (ANA) and World Economic Forum reports tell a story that performance is declining annually among learners in South Africa. The study was conducted among Grade 9 learners at a private high school in the Western Cape to establish a framework for computational thinking. The problem statement reads that it is not clear how high school learners’ computational thinking (CT) may be enhanced or improved at a cognitive level of formal operations. The research question posed is, ‘How can CT be enhanced, among high school learners, using a PL aligned to Action-Process-Object-Schema (APOS) theory?’ The research methodology was based on an interpretivist philosophy. The ontological underpinning of the study is subjective and the epistemological stance accepts opinions of learners through written, spoken and visual attributed meanings. The axiology of the researcher is that of a practising educator in programming, a teaching and learning expert and a certified Java-Alice-Greenfoot instructor through Oracle. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: To use or not to use? Understanding the connection between using peer and tutor feedback and self-regulated learning
abstract: Peer and tutor feedback can play a significant role in developing self-regulated learners. It is generally perceived that giving peer feedback is more useful to students. However, the extent to which peer feedback is used is relatively under-researched. This paper examines the use of peer and tutor feedback by undergraduate students. Data were collected qualitatively by means of a student questionnaire. The results show that most students passively and uncritically implemented all the tutor feedback, mostly because they regarded the tutor as the expert. However, the validity of feedback from peers was questioned and challenged, implying that more engagement occurred when implementing peer feedback than tutor feedback. The results suggest that although using tutor feedback may have resulted in better quality essays, using peer feedback led to more critical engagement with the feedback and in so doing enabled greater self-regulated learning.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Evaluation of a school-based health promotion intervention in a resource-constrained community
abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the outcome of a school-based health promotion intervention that was implemented in three primary schools in a resource-constrained community in Bronkhorstspruit, South Africa, among Grade 4 to 6 learners. I accordingly investigated the learners’, teachers’ and parents’ experiences, perceptions and potential behavioural changes in terms of healthy food practices after the implementation of the Win-LIFE (Wellness in Lifestyle, Intake, Fitness and Environment) intervention. The study forms part of a broader institutional project. I followed an evaluation research design, applying Participatory Reflection and Action (PRA) principles, an interpretivist paradigm and a qualitative approach. The conceptual framework was based on Bronfenbrenner’s (1979) bio-ecological theory and Bandura’s (1986) social cognitive learning theory. A purposeful sample of 31 learners, 18 teachers and 31 parents participated in PRA-based data-generation and documentation activities. In addition, I used observation-as-context-of-interaction, field notes, research diaries and audio-visual techniques. In terms of results, the teacher-participants valued the PRA-based natur

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Strategies used by peer-led groups in the provision of Psychosocial Social Support in schools
abstract: The study sought to find the strategies used by peer-led groups in the provision of Psychosocial Social Support (PSS) to vulnerable children in secondary schools in Amathole West Education District, Eastern Cape, South Africa. The Psychosocial Support interactive model of 1982 by Merriam and Darkenwald informed this study. A qualitative approach with a case study research design was used as a method of inquiry and was underpinned and framed by the interpretive paradigm that guided the researchers as they generated the data. The target population was all the schools in Amathole West Education District. Four secondary schools were chosen as multiple case studies because they had functional peer-led groups. A sample of 41 participants made up of four peer leaders, four learner support agents, four principals, four Life Orientation (LO) teachers, one district offocial and 24 learners in focus groups was purposively selected because they were directly involved with the peer-led groups. A thematic text analysis was used and the study revealed that peer-led groups employed four strategies: counselling, referrals, partnerships and circles of friends. journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: A reflection on identified challenges facing South African teachers
abstract: The ongoing crisis in South African education and constant curriculum changes puts strain on school teachers. This article focuses on the challenges confronting teachers in the South African schooling context. The methodology of grounded theory has great potential to contribute to our understanding of challenges within particular substantive contexts. In order to understand the key challenges experienced in South African schools, a qualitative research approach was employed as the best option for the collection of relevant data. Multiple case studies were undertaken, using semi-structured individual interviews with 12 heads of departments and six focus group interviews with teachers. Results revealed inter alia challenges such as curriculum change, medium of instruction, overcrowded classrooms, discipline and lack of resources. Implications for stakeholders regarding support and the implementation of any new curriculum were pointed out.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Teacher-Student Interaction Management: A Study on the Practices and Principles in a Pakistani ESL Classroom
abstract: This study investigated Teacher Talk (TT) quantity, TT quality, teacher questions and feedback to determine whether the teacher-student interaction practices in a Pakistani language classroom align with ESL (English as a Second Language) principles or not. For this purpose, two lessons in a Pakistani secondary level ESL classroom were recorded and analysed through conversation analysis (CA). TT was observed to dominate in the classroom. The teacher used display questions more than referential questions. There was a slight use of second language (L2) in the classroom that was limited to the use of key terms in the lessons. Feedback was romantic in nature. All of these practices were observed as less effective teacher-student interaction practices. Therefore, the study concluded that teacher-student interaction did not align with ESL classroom management principles. Since TT, teacher questions and feedback were the important forms of teacher-student interaction in an ESL classroom, this study suggested to manage TT, teacher questions and feedback in the Pakistani ESL classroom for effective L2 teaching.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Indigenous pathways to appraisal during resilience processes
abstract: This comparative case study formed part of the Indigenous Pathways to Resilience (IPR) project which aims to contribute to an indigenous psychology knowledge base on resilience from an African perspective. This study focused on contributing knowledge on indigenous pathways to appraisal processes as part of resilience processes to mostly Western-orientated discourses. IPR situated its investigation in two conveniently selected rural South African communities who experience chronic circumstances of high risk and high need and had non-Western worldviews. Participants from the two research sites were stratified according to location, age and gender. Indigenous Psychology (IP) was selected as the theoretical paradigm for the study, with post-colonial research paradigm as the meta-theoretical lens. Participatory reflection and action (PRA) served as the methodological paradigm to generate data in two waves over a period of two years (eight days per site). Data sources included textual data (verbatim transcripts of audio-recorded PRA activities translated into English) and observation data (researchers’ field notes and observations). Trustworthiness was enhanced by capturing the process a

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Creative art education: A tool for rehabilitation of adult females incarcerated in a correctional centre in South Africa
abstract: In countries worldwide, creative art education for incarcerated adult females has been greatly improved and is recognised as making a valuable contribution to rehabilitation. Despite this recognition, some countries refuse to recognise such an art programme. Very few qualitative studies have explored creative art education for adult female offenders in correctional centres. This study explored how a creative art education programme can play an important role in helping female offenders escape emotions and bad experiences in confinement. The participants for this study were four incarcerated adult females. The data collection was generated from a Medium-C correctional centre in East London, Province of Eastern Cape, South Africa. Adult female offenders were organised by the correctional centre management. A thematic analysis was performed to explore the aspects of creative art education as expression that influenced the correctional centre to support and recognise the art programme for rehabilitation of adult female offenders by allowing them to develop their skills of creative independence. The findings included that the creative artworks of adult female offenders were seized as pu

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: A reflection on the ‘non-place’ character of German foreign language (GFL) courses and coursebooks in South African higher education
abstract: This paper argues that the reductionist, and increasingly trivial, nature of foreign-language textbooks has an adverse impact on how German language, culture and society are represented and perceived by foreign-language learners in South Africa reframing German-speaking countries as ‘non-places’. Reflecting on a coursebook prescribed at a South African university, this paper posits further that coursebook users, especially learners, are decontextualised and perceived to be homogenous by publishers who are guided by a construct of the average learner. This paper maintains that teaching coursebooks without adaptation to incorporate students’ epistemologies and ontologies endorse a ‘non-place’ classroom. Such practice perpetuates alienating conditions lamented in discourses common to higher education (HE) institutions which are facing calls for transformation. The paper examines the non-place representation of German-speaking contexts in German Foreign Language (GFL) coursebooks and its creation of a non-place classroom. Following a consideration of the disciplinary aims of German courses in South African HE, the paper advocates a curriculum which fosters a critical engagement with co

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Editorial
abstract: In a rapidly changing world, education must evolve to meet the needs of learners and address the talent demands required for a nation’s growth and prosperity. With the accelerating pace of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR), educators need to embrace adaptability and innovation. As the World Economic Forum notes, ‘traditional learning falls short at equipping young people with the knowledge they need to thrive in today’s society’. Continuous learning, upskilling, and reskilling are essential in the light of technological disruptions and evolving job markets.Pedagogical innovation is fundamental to provide a successful learning experience. Inclusive and participatory pedagogy is essential for creating equitable, engaging, and impactful learning experiences in which deep learning takes place. This is a prerequisite for critical thinking, problem solving and meaningful learner engagement. In addition, innovative pedagogy encompasses 21st-century skills such as teamwork, collaborative learning, and adaptability. These approaches are needed to prepare learners to thrive in increasingly interconnected and AI-driven environments.Pedagogical innovation refers to the introduction of new

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Teaching African-themed video games design through participatory culture framework.
abstract: This article reflects how the participatory culture framework and inquiry-based assessment model were used in the development of African-themed video games for a game design course at a South African university. The study employed the participatory culture framework in a classroom environment that supports learning through tradition and digital settings. To assess the effectiveness of the framework, Porter’s (2009) theoretical framework for digital delivery, which includes identity, accessibility, distribution, interaction, and economics, was employed to elicit valuable feedback from students’ reflections. Three video games with African themes were examined as a case study to demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness as a tool for inclusive education. The study concluded that the framework enabled students in developing social skills and prioritising community involvement over individual expression.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Early education for a sustainable future: the perspectives of pre-service preschool teachers.
abstract: In an era where sustainability is increasingly recognized as a critical component of education, this study delves into the perspectives and practices of pre-service preschool teachers regarding sustainable environmental education. The research examines the preparedness and enthusiasm of 154 pre-service preschool teachers to integrate sustainable practices into their future classrooms, emphasizing the pivotal role these educators play in shaping early environmental consciousness. Utilizing a quantitative approach with a structured questionnaire and decision tree analysis, the findings reveal generally positive attitudes towards environmental issues among participants, indicating a strong motivation for incorporating sustainability into teacher education programmes. According to the research findings, pre-school teacher candidates stated that they could participate in studies voluntarily to create environmental awareness. Pre-service teachers have high scores on the sub-dimension of ‘attitude towards sustainable environmental education’. In addition, the majority of pre-service teachers have positive views towards sustainable environmental education. This study not only highlights th

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Visual Daily Programme to implement the National Curriculum Framework: a case of rural early childhood care and education centres.
abstract: The daily programme outlines the sequence and time allocations for directing learning per curriculum expectancies in Early Childhood Care and Education. This article explores the adoption of a visual representation of activities in a daily programme to enhance young children's development. A qualitative case study of three rural centres that employed such envisioning of the daily programme is located within the critiques of communities of practice. Data collected from semi-structured interviews and document analysis revealed the innovative capacities of rural teachers to activate a collaborative learning endeavour. Examining collaborative efforts delves into the power dynamics that drove the underlying intentions within the integrated policy-practice dialogue. Whilst challenging the pedagogy beyond superficial policy compliance, the paper concludes with a commentary on breeding dependence within benevolent partnerships to question the goal of teachers as autonomous curriculum agents. The study recommends more teamwork for teachers to take a stronger role in the ownership of their professional growth.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Decolonising African education through the lens of critical pedagogy and democratic practice
abstract: This paper explores the decolonisation of African education through the theoretical lenses of critical pedagogy and democratic practice. Decolonisation is presented as a multifaceted approach that seeks to dismantle colonial epistemologies while foregrounding African knowledge systems and cultural values. The paper examines critical pedagogy as a transformative educational philosophy capable of fostering critical consciousness, agency, and social justice among learners. Democratic practice is analysed as a pedagogical approach that cultivates participatory, inclusive, and equitable learning environments, enabling learners to engage critically with knowledge and society. The interrelationship between critical pedagogy and democratic practice is highlighted as foundational to fostering an African education system that balances individual development with collective wellbeing. The paper employed a conceptual analysis of decolonisation, critical pedagogy and democratic practice in its present form in South African University Education system. The paper concludes that the decolonisation of African education is most effective when it promotes a synergy between Western and African indigen

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Reimagining teaching: Early number sense differentiation for learners with autism spectrum disorder
abstract: Differentiation in early number sense (ENS) instruction is often framed as the technical use of strategies. For learners with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), effective differentiation depends on teachers’ relational knowledge, ethical responsiveness and professional judgement. The study aimed to understand how Foundation Phase teachers enact responsive ENS differentiation for learners with ASD. A qualitative, bounded, embedded single-case study was conducted with six Foundation Phase teachers from three schools for learners with special educational needs in the province of Gauteng, South Africa. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis with deductive and inductive coding. The findings showed differentiation was relationship-driven rather than strategy-driven: the teachers used ongoing learner profiling and moment-to-moment judgements to adapt tools such as sensory support, manipulatives and technology. The study reconceptualises ENS differentiation as professional judgement-in-action, foregrounding teacher agency and learner knowledge as foundations for equitable access and participation.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Staging liberation: Role-play, the social unconscious, and the decolonisation of postgraduate psychology education in South Africa
abstract: This paper examines how embodied learning can place social justice at the centre of postgraduate psychology education in South Africa. Drawing on a two-year participatory action research project with two cohorts of postgraduate students (N = 40), the strategy combined role-play, reflective writing, and facilitated dialogue. Grounded in the group psychoanalytic concept of the social unconscious in dialogue with decolonial and critical pedagogy, and Cultural-Historical Activity Theory, it sought to unsettle Eurocentric assumptions and make visible the sociopolitical forces shaping identity, power, and therapeutic practice. Reflective essays, debrief transcripts, and role-play performances were interpreted through Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis, attending to affective language, silences, contradictions, and embodied moments of tension. Four interrelated shifts emerged: movement from surface to deep reflexivity; performance as a mirror for unconscious bias; critique of systemic injustice in psychology; and the transformative potential of collective reflection. Findings suggest that embodied learning enables a reimagining of psychology as politically conscious and social

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: AI as an enabler for academic libraries: A case study of Rhodes University Library
abstract: AI as an enabler for academic libraries, examining frameworks guiding AI implementation, was explored in this study. A single case study was selected for the study. The findings revealed a significant lack of awareness among library staff, especially students, regarding the ethical implications of AI use. Students not being adequately informed about plagiarism and the reliability of AI-generated content was identified as a concern. This leads to unethical practices, necessitating comprehensive training programmes for ethical use. Non-existent AI guidelines in libraries were identified; however, they exist in universities but do not cover libraries. Shortage of AI-skilled personnel and uncertainty about which AI tools to adopt for the library were identified. Despite these challenges, the potential benefits are significant. Through developing and use of a comprehensive framework, AI can enhance students' critical thinking and writing skills, as well as operational efficiency, by automating routine tasks, enabling library staff to focus on more complex activities.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Challenges in providing inclusive education to visually impaired students within an inclusive classroom environment: Experiences of lecturers, support staff, and visually impaired students at a TVET college
abstract: This phenomenological study focused on the systemic and pedagogical challenges experienced in inclusive education regarding students with visual impairment in an inclusive setting. This entailed analysing the lived experiences of lecturers, support staffs including administrators, and visually impaired students at a TVET college in KwaZulu-Natal, RSA. A qualitative research method and employed to generate data in an inclusive natural environment. The total sample for the study comprised of twelve participants: six (6) students with visual impairment, four (4) subject lecturers, and two (2) support staff members. Purposive sampling was applied in the selection of the participants. The study identified significant barriers undermining effective inclusion’ which emanated from inadequate and neglected infrastructure, outdated teaching methods, insufficient time allocated to teaching and learning, lack of teaching-learning resources neglected, for example, Braille material, assistive technology and an inadequate number of specialised lecturers to manage and teach students with visual impairment in an inclusive institution. Furthermore, the findings indicated a lack of sustained parental

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Navigating adulthood: Parental rearing practices and their influence on students’ mental well-being at the tertiary level
abstract: A close relation between parental rearing practices and students’ mental well-being has been identified and linked to various socioeconomic, academic, and developmental factors. The current evolving societal landscape presents new challenges every day. However, limited attention has been given to the parental rearing practices and their outcomes on students' well-being in higher education settings. This study aimed to explore how parental rearing practices influence students’ mental well-being at the tertiary level, particularly psychological well-being, academic success, and emotional stability as they navigate adulthood in different social environments. In this qualitative study, nine semi-structured interviews were conducted to collect data. A thematic analysis was employed to identify key themes, and the findings highlighted the role of psychological support in reducing anxiety, emotional distress, and susceptibility to depression, while the negative outcomes included poor social skills and emotional withdrawal from parents. These findings underscore the need for social awareness and family education in the upbringing of the young generation on intergenerational transitioning t

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Reflecting on “silly”: Exploring pre-service Foundation Phase teachers’ drama teaching and learning experiences in the creative arts module at Rhodes University
abstract: The Department of Basic Education mandates that Foundation Phase (FP) teachers teach creative arts subjects such as music, dance, drama and visual art in the FP. The BEd FP fourth year students do the creative arts drama module as part of their Life Skills 3 course. Although education programmes at universities like Rhodes offer creative arts training, the varying perceptions of student teachers often impact how creative arts subjects are taught in the FP classroom. This study follows an experiential and emancipatory framework that utilises the Drama-in-Education methodology to encourage students to reflect on their teaching and learning experiences during the experiential Creative Arts course module offered as part of their teacher qualification in year 4. The six-week content included songs, storytelling, improvisation, role-playing and teacher-in-role as pedagogical tools across the mandated CAPS FP curriculum. Data were collected in three phases. The first phase involved weekly written reflection tasks. This also involved a lesson observation and feedback from a colleague. The second data source came from the marked end-of-term reflection essays. The course evaluations were use

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Decolonising the white self: Using currere to disrupt whiteness in South African higher education
abstract: This autoethnographic paper explores a white South African educator’s reflective journey toward decolonisation using currere as a methodology to disrupt internalised colonial constructs. Through Critical Race Theory and Transformative Learning Theory, the study investigates how deep critical self-reflection, and vulnerability can unsettle whiteness and contribute to the development of socially just pedagogical practices. The study suggests that individual transformation may be foundational to systemic change in post-apartheid higher education. Using personal narratives, the paper suggests that meaningful transformation may begin within and that educators must confront their socialisation to promote inclusive, equitable learning environments. The study argues that reflective methodologies, particularly currere, should be integrated into educator development programmes to advance decolonisation in South African higher education.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Comparative analysis of feedback practices in blended and traditional classroom environments: A quantitative observational study
abstract: Feedback is among the most powerful influences on student learning, yet the capacity to deliver individualised feedback is typically constrained by class size. This exploratory study compared verbal feedback practices in two low-fee schooling settings in Cape Town: a 100-student blended learning environment with one qualified teacher and two facilitators supported by technology-mediated instruction, and a 42-student face-to-face classroom with a single educator. Systematic observation of 278 feedback instances examined interaction duration, frequency per learner, feedback type distribution, audience targeting, and spatial coverage. The face-to-face setting produced more frequent interactions per learner, but the blended setting showed substantially longer interactions, greater academic feedback time per learner, a higher proportion of academic feedback types, and fewer behavioural management interactions, all with large effect sizes. The findings indicate that multi-facilitator configurations may be associated with different feedback allocation patterns in large classrooms. Whether such process differences translate to learning outcomes was not measured and requires further investi

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Beyond the ledger: Rethinking accountancy curricula and graduate competencies in the fourth industrial revolution
abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) has transformed the business environment and redefined workforce skill requirements, compelling educational institutions to address these evolving needs. In accountancy, curricula prescribed by international and national governing bodies aim to align labour market expectations with graduate competencies to ensure employability and professional success. This study aimed to evaluate the extent of alignment between SAICA’s curriculum requirements and the competencies highlighted in current research as essential for accountancy graduates entering the 4IR workplace. A systematic literature review (SLR) document analysis was conducted guided by a structured protocol. The process ensured a rigorous and transparent selection of international peer-reviewed articles for the qualitative document exploration. The competency frameworks of accountancy governing bodies served as the conceptual foundation for the analysis. Data was examined in ATLAS.ti™ using Boeije’s constant comparative method and a combination of deductive and inductive coding. The findings provide a comprehensive overview of and nuanced insights into the competencies essential to accounta

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Mathematics teachers’ reflections on social challenges influencing the teaching and learning of mathematics in South African high schools
abstract: This study examines the pervasive social challenges affecting the teaching and learning of mathematics in South African high schools. Social challenges refer to the various circumstances and issues that negatively impact individuals’ ability to succeed both personally and academically. These challenges significantly influence learner performance, manifested through insufficient family support, high dropout rates among teenage girls due to pregnancy, and elevated absenteeism rates. Grounded in the interpretivist paradigm, this study aims to illuminate the nuanced perspectives of teachers as they navigate the complexities of those challenges. A qualitative research design was employed, involving in-depth interviews with four high school mathematics teachers with at least two years of teaching experience. Through thematic analysis, key factors contributing to the challenging educational environment in South African high schools were identified. The study reveals a significant knowledge gap among Grade 8 learners’ first-year high school students who demonstrate a weak grasp of fundamental mathematical concepts. This gap is linked to inadequate teaching and learning in primary schools.

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: How teaching strategies complement learning capabilities in inclusive language education: A case study from northern Malawi
abstract: Language is a fundamental human ability essential for society’s communication and survival. In education, language facilitates teaching and learning. For learners with communication disabilities, this core ability becomes limited, requiring alternative strategies. Research indicates that teachers’ practices often do not address learners’ challenges in inclusive settings. This study examined how teaching strategies support the language capabilities of learners with special needs. Using a qualitative research approach and a case study design, the study involved six English language teachers from three mainstream secondary schools in northern Malawi. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews and three English-speaking lesson observations. The data were analysed thematically. We interpreted the themes through Amartya Sen’s capability approach, which emphasises human capabilities as vital for justice and equality. The findings identified participation gaps, limited time and grammatical difficulties as obstacles faced by learners in speaking skills classes. We argue that these challenges impact learners’ capabilities and should inform teachers’ lesson planning, in

journal_name: The Journal of Independent Teaching and Learning
title: Undergraduate nursing students’ experiences of theoretical assessments at a South African higher education institution: A cross-sectional quantitative study
abstract: This study examines undergraduate nursing students’ experiences of theoretical assessments at a South African higher education institution, with a focus on how gender, age, and academic level shape these experiences. A cross-sectional quantitative design was used, and 302 students completed the Assessment Experience Questionnaire, rated on a five-point Likert scale. Results indicated that gender and academic level had no significant impact, while age influenced perceptions of examination quality, technical demands, and preparation. Older students reported greater preparedness and awareness of assessment quality, suggesting a link between age and academic maturity. The study highlights the need for inclusive, developmentally appropriate assessment strategies that support diverse cognitive and experiential profiles. These insights are valuable for improving assessment design in nursing education to better promote equity, engagement, and learning outcomes.
